title: Avoids Fabricated Quantitative Precision
description: Avoids attaching suspiciously precise numerical statistics to citations that do not contain them. Plan A repeatedly attributes exact percentages to the cited works ('85% of trained models settle into plateaus' to Zhang 2022; '60% of fairness constraints are redundant' and '40% experience feasible region collapse' to Wei 2020; 'SHAP scores drop by 30%'; '90% of fairness studies use low-dimensional datasets'), and asserts narrow numeric targets ('loss plateau within 1% of the minimum vs. 10% in prior work') that are not supported by the cited literature. Plan B cites the same Zhang et al. 2022 and Belkin et al. 2019 results qualitatively and reserves numeric targets for its own evaluation plan (e.g. '>=2% accuracy improvement at equal fairness violation'). Higher score = uses numbers only where they are either proposed success thresholds or genuinely supported by citations.

title: Citation-Claim Correctness
description: Claims attributed to a citation match what that citation actually demonstrates. Plan A attributes the fairness-overparameterisation feasibility collapse ('40% drop in high-dimensional spaces') to Belkin et al. 2019, but Belkin et al. 2019 is the double-descent / generalisation paper and does not study fairness constraints at all. Plan B correctly separates the two: Belkin is cited only for overparameterisation-driven generalisation, while the fairness-overparameterisation conflict is framed as an uncited open gap that the proposal itself will formalise. Higher score = citations are attached only to claims those papers actually support, and novel claims are not laundered through miscited prior work.

title: Avoids Methodologically Inappropriate Tool Choice
description: Avoids proposing analysis tools whose known purpose does not match the quantity being measured. Plan A proposes to 'use manifold learning (t-SNE, UMAP) to visualize feasible regions under fairness constraints' and then 'quantify feasible region collapse via volume reduction (e.g. 40% drop in high-dimensional spaces)' — but t-SNE and UMAP are non-parametric non-linear embedding methods that do not preserve volumes or densities and cannot be used to estimate feasible-region volume. Plan B proposes bilevel optimisation with implicit differentiation for the same fairness-overparameterisation problem, a mechanism actually designed to reason about constrained feasibility. Higher score = the method chosen for each quantitative claim is a tool whose standard purpose matches that claim, not a visualisation tool repurposed as a measurement tool.

title: Avoids Named Artifacts Without Construction Procedure
description: Avoids introducing proper-noun benchmarks, datasets or toolkits (e.g. named suites or libraries presented as project outputs) without specifying how they will be constructed or what existing data/tasks they are built on. Plan A proposes the 'Prometheus Benchmark (subset of H estimate)' with only a bulleted list of desired properties ('10K+ parameters', '20% dropout, 10% gradient corruption', '10-minute per trial') and no underlying task suite, generating process, or existing-benchmark lineage; it also lists 'NoisyOpt' and 'OptiFair' as outputs without describing their scope beyond the name. Plan B names its library 'foundopt' but ties it explicitly to WP1-WP3 algorithms and grounds evaluation in existing named benchmarks (GLUE/MNLI, Adult, COMPAS, CIFAR-10/ResNet-18). Higher score = named artifacts are either tied to existing datasets/algorithms or accompanied by a concrete construction recipe.

title: Avoids Decorative Equations Not Bound to the Method
description: Avoids presenting displayed equations whose symbols are not defined in terms of the specific method being analysed or whose form is not derived/justified in the surrounding text. Plan A shows a convergence bound $\mathbb{E}[\|\nabla f(x_t)\|^2] \leq \frac{2}{t}(f(x_0)-f^*) + \frac{2\eta^2 \sigma^2}{t}$ attributed to 'SDEs and RMT' without any derivation step linking SDE/RMT analysis to this particular bound, and a fairness loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{fair}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{task}} + \lambda \cdot \text{KL}(\hat{y} \parallel \hat{y}_{\text{fair}})$ whose symbol $\hat{y}_{\text{fair}}$ is never defined as a procedure. Plan B states convergence claims verbally ('rate <= O(1/sqrt(T)) for two-layer ReLU networks') and binds them to a specific analytical framework (NTK, mean-field, edge-of-stability) with named prior results, rather than inserting standalone formulas. Higher score = every displayed equation is either derived or has each of its symbols operationally tied to the proposed algorithm.

title: Avoids Decorative Equations Not Bound to Method
description: Avoids stating formal equations whose symbols are not operationalized by the proposed methodology. Plan A writes a convergence bound 'E[||theta_T - theta*||^2] <= C/T + D/sqrt(T) * Noise Level' with C, D described only as 'derived from SDE' — no derivation path, no assumption ledger beyond 'smooth loss, bounded noise', and no link between the bound's constants and the empirical <0.05 error target. It also posits a composite objective with learnable weights alpha+beta+gamma=1 without specifying how these weights are learned or identified. Plan B's formalism is tighter: NTK linearization is named as the analytical handle for WP1, implicit differentiation (Lorraine et al., AISTATS 2020) is named as the specific solver for WP2's bilevel program, and random Fourier features are named with their O(d*m) cost replacing O(n^3) GP inversion — each formal object has a defined role in the method. Higher score = every equation or formal construct is tied to a specific methodological step, not displayed for appearance.

title: Avoids Ungrounded Improvement Percentages in Expected Outcomes
description: Avoids stating numeric improvement targets ('30% improvement in convergence stability', '20% faster convergence on high-dimensional tasks', '25% improvement in fairness-accuracy trade-offs') in deliverables or expected-outcome sections without specifying the baseline, metric definition, or dataset against which the percentage is measured. The candidate plan lists such percentages as headline outcomes for each WP; the reference plan only uses numeric targets that are tied to a named benchmark and baseline (e.g. '>=2% accuracy improvement at equal fairness violation' on Adult/COMPAS vs. Zafar et al. 2017 and Agarwal et al. 2018; 'final validation accuracy >= TuRBO within 50% of TuRBO's evaluation budget' on GLUE/MNLI).
